incertitudes: Question 6 (i)(b) : le résultat imprimé « v = (80/k)(1 - e^{-kt}) » est incompatible avec (a) tel qu'imprimé (dv/dt = (80 - kv)/8) : l'intégration donne v = (80/k)(1 - e^{-kt/8}). Le résultat imprimé serait exact si dv/dt valait 80 - kv avec v limite 80/k (par exemple pour une masse de 1 kg). Le corrigé démontre la forme correcte et signale l'écart au lieu de forcer l'identité. Le sujet ne dit pas que la particule part du repos : v = 0 à t = 0 est supposé (chute « freely »).

Question 6 (ii) : les positions r1 et r2 sont lues comme des vecteurs positions par rapport à l'origine O ; le moment résultant est celui autour de O (scalaire, sens antihoraire positif). Le sujet imprime « Take g as 10 m s^-2 » : valeur retenue g = 10 (8g = 80 N).

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $8\ \mathrm{kg}$ falls freely under gravity through a medium whose resistance to motion is $kv$, where $v$ is the speed of the particle and $k$ is a positive constant. (Take $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.) Prove that after time $t$ seconds $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{80 - kv}{8}$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Model.** The particle moves in a vertical line. Take the downward direction as positive. Two forces act on the particle: the weight $mg = 8\times 10 = 80\ \mathrm{N}$ downwards, and the resistance $kv$ upwards (it opposes the motion).

**Newton's second law** (net force in the positive direction $=$ mass $\times$ acceleration, with acceleration $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$):

$$8\,\frac{dv}{dt} = 80 - kv \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{80 - kv}{8}$$

as required.

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle of mass $8\ \mathrm{kg}$ falls freely under gravity through a medium whose resistance to motion is $kv$, where $v$ is the speed of the particle and $k$ is a positive constant, and $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{80 - kv}{8}$ (take $g$ as $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$). Hence show that the speed of the particle at time $t$ seconds is $\dfrac{80}{k}\left(1 - e^{-kt}\right)$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Solving the differential equation.** The particle falls from rest, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$. Separate the variables ($80 - kv > 0$ because the speed never exceeds $\tfrac{80}{k}$):

$$\int_0^v \frac{dv}{80 - kv} = \int_0^t \frac{dt}{8}$$

$$-\frac{1}{k}\Big[\ln(80 - kv)\Big]_0^v = \frac{t}{8} \;\Rightarrow\; \ln\frac{80 - kv}{80} = -\frac{kt}{8}$$

$$80 - kv = 80\,e^{-kt/8} \;\Rightarrow\; v = \frac{80}{k}\left(1 - e^{-kt/8}\right)$$

**Check.** $v = 0$ at $t = 0$, and $v \to \tfrac{80}{k}$ (the terminal speed, where the resistance balances the weight) as $t \to \infty$. Differentiating, $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 10\,e^{-kt/8}$ and $\dfrac{80 - kv}{8} = \dfrac{80\,e^{-kt/8}}{8} = 10\,e^{-kt/8}$, so the differential equation is satisfied.

**Remark on the printed result.** The form $v = \tfrac{80}{k}(1 - e^{-kt})$ asked for in the question has the exponent $-kt$, whereas the equation proved in (a), $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{80 - kv}{8}$, gives the exponent $-\dfrac{kt}{8}$. The printed form would correspond to $\dfrac{dv}{dt} = 80 - kv$ (for instance a particle of mass $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ with $mg = 80$), so the exponent $-kt$ is a misprint for $-kt/8$ (the mass $8\ \mathrm{kg}$ divides $k$). From the given data the correct result is

**$v = \dfrac{80}{k}\left(1 - e^{-kt/8}\right)$**, with the same terminal speed $\dfrac{80}{k}$ as in the printed formula.

questions.enonce_markdown: Forces $\mathbf{F}_1 = (7\mathbf{i} - 3\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2 = (\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{N}$ act at points with position vectors $\mathbf{r}_1 = (4\mathbf{i} - 5\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{m}$ and $\mathbf{r}_2 = (3\mathbf{i} - 8\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{m}$ respectively. Find the magnitude of the resultant moment.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The forces and position vectors all lie in the $xy$-plane, so each moment about the origin $O$ is $\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F} = (xF_y - yF_x)\,\mathbf{k}$ (positive $=$ anticlockwise).

$$\mathbf{r}_1\times\mathbf{F}_1:\quad 4(-3) - (-5)(7) = -12 + 35 = 23\ \mathrm{N\,m}$$

$$\mathbf{r}_2\times\mathbf{F}_2:\quad 3(-5) - (-8)(1) = -15 + 8 = -7\ \mathrm{N\,m}$$

The resultant moment is the sum:

$$G = 23 + (-7) = 16\ \mathrm{N\,m}\ \text{(anticlockwise, along } +\mathbf{k})$$

**Magnitude of the resultant moment $= 16\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.**
